body: The background legacy write takes its context from the request `ctx`. The apiserver cancels the request context as soon as the handler returns, which happens right after this goroutine starts. So the legacy Create will usually fail with `context canceled`, and the 'safe measure' write to legacy mostly never happens. Start from `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)`, which keeps the values (identity/namespace/logger) but drops the cancellation, and then add the 10s timeout. The same bug is in Delete (L110), Update (L135) and DeleteCollection (L163).

When the unified-storage Create fails, this records a *legacy* duration, but legacy was never called. It should be `recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`. Otherwise the storage error metrics under-count and the legacy metrics show phantom errors.
Same metric mix-up as in Create: a unified-storage Update failure is recorded with `recordLegacyDuration`. It should be `recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`.

This goroutine measures the *legacy* DeleteCollection but records it with `recordStorageDuration`. The legacy call's latency and errors end up in the storage histogram, and no legacy metric is recorded at all. Use `recordLegacyDuration`.

The label here is `name` (the object name), not `options.Kind` as in every other call. Besides being inconsistent, this creates one Prometheus series per deleted object name, which is unbounded label cardinality.

`klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` stores the base logger rather than the `log` built on the line above, so the name/kind/method values are lost for downstream logging. It should be `klog.NewContext(ctx, log)`.

The legacy error (`errObjectSt`) is thrown away and never logged, here and in the other async goroutines. Divergence between unified and legacy storage then only shows up as a metric bool, with no way to find which object failed or why. Log the error with the object name/kind.

`obj` is handed to `Legacy.Create` in a background goroutine after `Storage.Create` has already run on it. Storage implementations often mutate the input in place (they set UID, resourceVersion, creationTimestamp), and `created` is often the same pointer. That causes two problems: (1) legacy receives an object carrying unified-storage metadata such as resourceVersion, which legacy Create may reject; (2) the goroutine reads, and legacy may mutate, the object at the same time the handler serializes `created` for the response, which is a data race. Pass a DeepCopy made before the goroutine starts, and ideally base it on `created`.

The original `objInfo` is replayed against legacy. The earlier code (and modes 1/2) wrapped it in `updateWrapper` so legacy received the object as it was actually stored in unified storage. Now `UpdatedObject` is computed against legacy's copy of the object, and any preconditions or resourceVersion in the request refer to unified storage's RV. Legacy updates can therefore conflict or produce a different result from what was stored. Wrap it as `&updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: res}`. A related issue: because these writes are fire-and-forget goroutines with no ordering, two quick updates or an update followed by a delete can reach legacy out of order and leave it permanently inconsistent.

The Delete behavior changed. Previously a NotFound from unified storage was tolerated and the delete still went through to legacy. Now a NotFound in unified storage returns immediately and legacy is never touched. Objects that exist only in legacy (for example, created before migration and not yet copied) can't be deleted in mode 3 and stay behind in legacy.

The async legacy goroutine can still be running when the test returns. The mock gets called after the test has finished (and after `mock.AssertExpectations` would have run), which makes the test racy/flaky and means the legacy calls are never really checked. Also, the 'unified store fails' case only sets up a Create expectation through `setupLegacyFn`. It only passes because legacy and storage share one mock, so the test doesn't check what its name says.
